hints: Look closely at leaf alcohol, it has two different functional groups that could react, so ask which one acidified dichromate actually attacks.
Check the alcohol end first, it is a primary $-CH_2OH$ group heated with excess oxidant, so think what it must become.
Now ask if the $C=C$ double bond in the middle survives this reagent, and keep only the product where that part is unchanged.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two functional groups**

Leaf alcohol has both an alkene and a primary alcohol in one molecule. Think of them separately.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Oxidise the primary alcohol with excess**

A primary alcohol is first oxidised to an aldehyde, then with excess hot oxidant straight on to a carboxylic acid.

$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{R-CHO} \rightarrow \text{R-CO}_2\text{H}$$

**Check what happens to the C=C bond**

This is the key Cambridge distinction. Hot acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ oxidises alcohols but does NOT cleave $C=C$ double bonds. Cleavage to two acids needs hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$.

So the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CHCH}_2-$ part stays exactly as it is.

**Put it together**

Only the $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ end changes to $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, giving an unsaturated carboxylic acid.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$$

options.A: Incorrect. This shows addition of two -OH groups across the double bond plus oxidation of the alcohol. That diol formation needs cold, dilute alkaline KMnO4, not acidified K2Cr2O7, which leaves C=C alone.
options.B: Incorrect. This changes the C=C into two C=O ketone groups. Acidified dichromate does not do this to alkenes. Students sometimes confuse oxidation of alcohols with attack on the double bond.
options.C: Correct. The primary alcohol $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ is fully oxidised by excess hot reagent to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, while the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH-}$ alkene portion is untouched by dichromate.
options.D: Incorrect. These are the oxidative cleavage products from breaking the C=C bond. That vigorous cleavage requires hot concentrated KMnO4, not K2Cr2O7(aq), so this is a classic reagent-confusion trap.
